entries.topicDescription: Communication primitives for coroutines — send and receive values between concurrent tasks.

tips.title: Fan-out lets multiple coroutines compete for values from one channel
tips.content:
Launching several coroutines that all receive from the same channel
distributes the work automatically — each value sent is delivered to
exactly one of the competing receivers, giving you a worker-pool pattern
without any manual load-balancing logic.

This is useful for parallelizing processing of a stream of work items
where order doesn't matter and you want N workers consuming from a shared
queue.

tips.title: Fan-in merges several producer channels into a single consumer stream
tips.content:
When multiple independent sources need to feed one processing pipeline,
running a separate consumer per source duplicates the downstream logic.

Launching one coroutine per producer that forwards into a shared output
channel merges all sources into a single stream a single consumer can
process uniformly, without the consumer needing to know how many
producers exist.

tips.title: select {} multiplexes across several channel operations at once
tips.content:
Waiting on multiple channels with separate blocking receive() calls forces
you to process them in a fixed order, even if a later channel has data
ready first.

select {} suspends until any one of several registered clauses (onReceive,
onSend, a Deferred's onAwait) becomes ready, and runs only that clause —
letting you react to whichever source is ready first, similar to a
multi-way non-blocking select() in networking code.

tips.title: Build an actor manually with a channel and a processing loop
tips.content:
The old actor{} coroutine builder is deprecated, but the actor pattern —
serializing access to mutable state by funneling all mutations through
one channel and a single consuming coroutine — is still a valid,
supported approach when built manually.

Because only one coroutine ever reads from the channel and mutates the
state, there's no need for locks; concurrency safety comes from the
single-consumer design itself.

tips.title: onUndeliveredElement prevents resource leaks on channel cancellation
tips.content:
If a channel holding closeable resources (file handles, subscriptions) is
cancelled or closed while elements are still buffered, those elements are
simply dropped — nothing closes them automatically, which leaks the
underlying resource.

Passing an onUndeliveredElement lambda to Channel()'s constructor registers
a cleanup callback invoked for every element that never reaches a
receiver, whether due to cancellation, an exception, or the channel
closing early.
tips.codeSnippet:
val channel = Channel<Connection>(capacity = 16, onUndeliveredElement = { conn -> conn.close() })
// any Connection stuck in the buffer when cancelled gets closed automatically

tips.title: close(cause) vs cancel() have different consumer-visible semantics
tips.content:
channel.close() (no cause) lets consumers finish draining any already-
buffered elements before the for-loop ends normally — it's a graceful
shutdown signal. channel.close(cause) still drains buffered elements, but
the consumer's iteration eventually throws that cause once drained.

channel.cancel() is more aggressive: it immediately discards any buffered
elements and makes all pending and future receive attempts fail right
away, rather than draining first — use cancel() when buffered data is no
longer relevant, not just to signal completion.
tips.codeSnippet:
channel.close() // consumers finish draining buffered values, then exit the for-loop
channel.close(IOException("connection lost")) // drains, then throws after
channel.cancel() // buffered values discarded immediately, receivers fail right away

tips.title: Prefer SharedFlow over BroadcastChannel for hot multicast streams
tips.content:
BroadcastChannel is deprecated in favor of SharedFlow, which solves the
same 'one value, many subscribers' problem with clearer backpressure
semantics (replay cache, extraBufferCapacity, and an explicit
onBufferOverflow strategy) instead of BroadcastChannel's less flexible
conflation-only behavior.

SharedFlow is also better integrated with the rest of the Flow API,
letting you apply standard operators to a hot multicast stream instead of
working with a separate Channel-based API surface.

tips.title: Pipeline pattern chains channels through coroutines for streaming transforms
tips.content:
Processing a large stream through several sequential transformation
steps (parse, validate, enrich, persist) as one monolithic loop makes it
hard to parallelize individual stages or reason about them independently.

A channel-based pipeline has each stage be its own coroutine reading from
one channel and writing to the next — each stage can run concurrently
with the others, and stages naturally backpressure upstream if a buffered
channel fills up.

tips.title: CONFLATED channels implement backpressure by keeping only the latest value
tips.content:
A rendezvous or bounded channel applies backpressure by making the sender
suspend when the consumer falls behind — but sometimes only the most
recent value matters (live location updates, current UI state), and
older unconsumed values are just noise.

Channel(Channel.CONFLATED) never suspends the sender; instead, sending a
new value while an old one is still unconsumed silently overwrites it —
the consumer only ever sees the latest state, never a backlog.

tips.title: produce{} combines channel creation and coroutine launch into one call
tips.content:
Manually creating a Channel and separately launching a coroutine to fill
it is boilerplate that's easy to get slightly wrong — forgetting to close
the channel, or launching in the wrong scope.

The produce{} coroutine builder returns a ReceiveChannel directly, runs
the given block in a new coroutine bound to the calling scope, and
automatically closes the channel when the block completes or the
coroutine is cancelled.

tips.title: Closing a channel tells receivers no more values are coming
tips.content:
A channel that's never closed leaves receivers waiting (suspended)
indefinitely once the producer is done, since `for (value in channel)`
only ends when the channel closes.

Calling channel.close() after the last send() lets any active or future
for-loop over the channel finish cleanly instead of hanging forever.

tips.title: trySend and tryReceive never suspend, unlike send and receive
tips.content:
send() and receive() are suspend functions — they pause the coroutine if
the channel isn't ready (full or empty). Sometimes you need to attempt an
operation without suspending at all, such as inside a non-suspending
callback.

trySend()/tryReceive() attempt the operation immediately and return a
ChannelResult indicating success or failure, instead of suspending — useful
when suspension isn't possible at the call site.
